influences.name: Christ as Sol, Orpheus and the Good Shepherd in early art
influences.sourceCulture: Graeco-Roman pastoral, Orphic and solar imagery: the ram-bearing shepherd (kriophoros), Orpheus taming the beasts, and Helios/Sol in his chariot
influences.christianForm: Christ depicted as the Good Shepherd, as a new Orpheus and as the radiant ‘Sun of righteousness’ in catacomb, sarcophagus and tomb art
influences.evidenceNote: The borrowing of visual types is well documented: the shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders, Orpheus with his lyre and Sol in a quadriga all existed in Roman art long before Christians used them, and Christian examples sit beside pagan ones in the same workshops and cemeteries. What was borrowed was a visual vocabulary, not a cult: the meanings Christians gave these images came from Psalm 23, John 10, Luke 15 and Malachi 4:2.
influences.popularClaim: Early Christian art proves that Jesus was really a sun god or a rebranded pagan deity, because the earliest pictures of him are copied from Apollo, Orpheus and Sol Invictus.
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Historians agree that pre-Constantinian Christian art took over existing Roman image types, as any new art in the Roman world had to; workshops produced sarcophagi with shepherds and seasons for pagan and Christian buyers alike. The ‘Good Shepherd’ is by far the commonest image of Christ before 313, and its biblical meaning is explicit in texts of the period. Orpheus images are rare and appear also in Jewish art (David as Orpheus in the Dura-Europos synagogue). The single famous ‘Christ-Helios’ mosaic, in the Mausoleum of the Julii beneath St Peter’s, is identified as Christ only because of the Jonah and fisherman scenes around it, and some scholars read it as Sol. Writers such as Clement of Alexandria consciously used Orpheus and the sun as metaphors for Christ, while Leo the Great complained of Christians who still bowed to the sun: the evidence shows adaptation of imagery and occasional popular confusion, not a solar origin for Christian belief.
influences.summary: The first Christian images of Christ borrowed the familiar Roman figures of the shepherd carrying a sheep, the singer Orpheus and the sun-god in his chariot, re-reading them through biblical texts about the Good Shepherd and the ‘Sun of righteousness’.
influences.story:
Christian art appears in the archaeological record only around AD 200, in the catacombs of Rome, on sarcophagi and in the house church at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates (decorated c. 232–256). It did not invent a new visual language. Its artists and patrons used the stock repertoire of Roman funerary art: banquets, orants (praying figures with raised hands), seasons, vines, fishermen and, above all, the youthful shepherd carrying a sheep across his shoulders. This kriophoros (‘ram-bearer’) type had a long pagan history, from archaic Greek votive statues to Calamis’s Hermes Kriophoros at Tanagra described by Pausanias, and in Roman art it had become a generic emblem of rural peace and philanthropy.

For Christians the figure carried precise biblical meaning: ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 10:11), the shepherd who seeks the lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7), and the Lord who is ‘my shepherd’ in Psalm 23, a psalm associated with baptism and burial. Tertullian, c. 210–220, mentions the shepherd painted on Christian communion cups (De pudicitia 7 and 10), and the shepherd appears in the baptistery at Dura beside Adam and Eve. Robin Jensen counts the Good Shepherd as the most frequently depicted image of Christ before Constantine; only in the late fourth century, as Christ came to be shown enthroned and bearded, did the type fade.

Orpheus, the mythical singer whose music tamed wild beasts and who descended to the underworld, appears in a handful of Roman catacomb paintings (Domitilla, Callixtus, Peter and Marcellinus) and on some sarcophagi. Clement of Alexandria opens his Exhortation to the Greeks (c. 195) by contrasting Orpheus with Christ, the true singer of the ‘New Song’ who tames the wildest beasts, human beings. Jewish artists made the same move: the synagogue at Dura-Europos shows David playing the lyre in the pose of Orpheus. The image was a shared Mediterranean way of picturing harmony and the conquest of death, adopted by communities who gave it their own scriptural content.

Solar imagery is the most contested case. Malachi 4:2 promised the ‘sun of righteousness’ rising with healing in its wings, the Gospels describe Christ’s face shining ‘like the sun’ at the Transfiguration, and Christians prayed facing east. Clement calls Christ ‘the Sun of righteousness who drives his chariot over all’ (Protrepticus 11). In the Vatican necropolis, the mid-third-century Mausoleum M, the ‘Tomb of the Julii’, has a gold mosaic of a charioteer with rays behind his head, surrounded by Jonah, a fisherman and a shepherd; most scholars identify it as Christ-Helios, though Steven Hijmans and others caution that the figure is iconographically pure Sol. Pagan critics noticed the parallel: Tertullian reports that some thought the Christians worshipped the sun because they prayed eastwards and kept the ‘day of the sun’ (Apology 16; Ad nationes 1.13), a charge he rejects.

The church’s leaders were alert to the risk of confusion. Pope Leo the Great, preaching at Christmas c. 450 (Sermon 27), rebuked Christians who turned and bowed to the rising sun on the steps of St Peter’s before entering the basilica. The Council of Elvira (c. 306) had already ruled that pictures should not be painted on church walls, and a letter attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea discouraged images of Christ altogether. The verdict of modern scholarship, from André Grabar to Thomas Mathews and Jensen, is that early Christian art is a classic case of the borrowing of forms: Christians spoke the visual language of their culture while insisting, in their texts, on meanings drawn from Israel’s scriptures and the story of Jesus.
howItHappened: Christians bought sarcophagi and paid painters from the same Roman workshops as their pagan neighbours, choosing from an existing stock of motifs.
Ambiguous pastoral images (shepherds, vines, banquets) were selected because they could be read biblically without advertising a persecuted faith.
Apologists such as Clement of Alexandria and Justin presented Christ as the fulfilment of what was best in Greek myth and philosophy, encouraging visual parallels.
Biblical metaphors (shepherd, light, sun of righteousness) gave Christians a reason to adopt pagan types and fill them with new meaning.
From the later fourth century imperial and enthroned images of Christ displaced the youthful shepherd type.
examples: Good Shepherd fresco in the baptistery of the Dura-Europos house church (c. 232–256), now at Yale University Art Gallery.
Good Shepherd ceiling paintings in the Catacombs of Priscilla and Callixtus, Rome (third century).
Christ-Helios (or Sol) mosaic in the Mausoleum of the Julii, Vatican necropolis (mid-third century).
Orpheus among the animals in the Catacomb of Domitilla and the Catacomb of Peter and Marcellinus, Rome.
Marble Good Shepherd statuettes of the third and fourth centuries in the Vatican Museo Pio Cristiano.
The Good Shepherd mosaic in the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Ravenna (c. 425–450), where the shepherd is now robed in gold and purple.

defenders.name: Clement of Alexandria
defenders.text: Presented Christ as the true Orpheus and the ‘Sun of righteousness’ (Protrepticus 1 and 11), and in the Paedagogus (3.11) advised Christians which existing seal-ring motifs they could use.

defenders.name: Justin Martyr
defenders.text: Argued that the Word had sown ‘seeds’ of truth among the Greeks, a theology that made borrowing classical forms appear legitimate (2 Apology 13).

defenders.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
defenders.text: Freely used solar and imperial light imagery for Christ and the Logos in his orations, even while doubting the propriety of portraits of Christ.

critics.name: Leo the Great
critics.text: Rebuked Christians who bowed to the rising sun on the steps of St Peter’s before Christmas Mass, as a relic of pagan sun worship (Sermon 27.4).

critics.name: Council of Elvira
critics.text: Canon 36 (c. 306) ruled that there should be no pictures in churches, ‘lest what is worshipped and adored be painted on walls’.

critics.name: Tertullian
critics.text: Rejected the pagan charge that Christians worshipped the sun (Apology 16), and as a Montanist mocked the shepherd painted on the cups of lax Christians (De pudicitia 10).

keptBy: Catholic and Orthodox churches, which continue to use the Good Shepherd and ‘Sun of righteousness’ imagery in art and hymnody.
Anglican and Lutheran churches, in stained glass and liturgical art.
Protestant churches generally, in the Good Shepherd as a devotional and pastoral theme.
rejectedBy: Strict Reformed iconoclasts of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, who removed images of Christ from churches on the basis of the second commandment.
Some modern ‘pagan origins’ writers, who treat the borrowed imagery as evidence that Christ was a sun god.

influences.name: The halo (nimbus) and imperial imagery
influences.sourceCulture: The radiate crown and luminous disc around the heads of Helios/Sol, other deities and, from the third and fourth centuries, Roman emperors
influences.christianForm: The nimbus around Christ, the Virgin, angels and saints, including the cruciform nimbus reserved for Christ and the square nimbus for living donors
influences.evidenceNote: The halo is a well-documented visual borrowing. It is absent from the earliest Christian art, appears on Christ only from the mid-fourth century, and spreads to angels, the Virgin and saints in the fifth and sixth centuries, exactly when it was standard for gods and emperors in Roman art. It was adopted as a sign of glory and holiness, not as a sign of sun worship.
influences.popularClaim: The halo is a pagan sun disc, proof that Christian saints are sun gods in disguise (a claim popularised by Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons, 1853).
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Art historians agree that the nimbus came from classical art, where Helios, Apollo, Mithras, Isis and other deities, and later emperors such as Constantine and Theodosius I, were shown with radiate crowns or discs of light. Christian artists did not use it in the third century; they took it up after Constantine, when it had become a general sign of exalted status, and gave it biblical content: the shining face of Moses (Exodus 34:29), the transfigured Christ whose face ‘shone like the sun’ (Matthew 17:2), and the righteous who ‘will shine like the sun’ (Matthew 13:43). Because emperors themselves appear nimbate in Christian churches (Justinian at San Vitale), the halo in late antiquity marked rank and sacral authority as well as personal sanctity. It is a borrowing of form whose meaning was redefined, not evidence of a solar cult.
influences.summary: The halo was borrowed from Graeco-Roman portrayals of gods and emperors in the fourth century and became Christianity’s standard sign of holiness, reinterpreted through biblical images of divine glory and light.
influences.story:
In Greek and Roman art a ring or rays of light around the head signalled divinity or heroic status. Helios and Sol wore the radiate crown; Hellenistic kings imitated it on coins; Roman emperors from Nero onwards were shown with the radiate crown on coinage, and by the late third and fourth centuries emperors were depicted with a plain disc of light, the nimbus, as a sign of their quasi-divine majesty. The same convention travelled east: Kushan kings and the Buddha of Gandharan art received haloes from the shared Hellenistic and Iranian repertoire.

The earliest Christian art, from c. 200 to the early fourth century, has no haloes at all: the Good Shepherd, Jonah and the orants of the catacombs are bare-headed. The nimbus first appears around Christ in the middle and later fourth century, in catacomb paintings such as the bust of Christ in the Catacomb of Commodilla and in apse mosaics. Over the following two centuries it was extended to angels, the Lamb, the Virgin Mary, apostles and saints. The chronology matters: Christians adopted the halo only after it had become a widely used sign of glory and rank, at a time when emperors were also routinely nimbate.

The imperial dimension is unmistakable. The silver Missorium of Theodosius (388) shows Theodosius I and his co-emperors with haloes. In the sanctuary of San Vitale in Ravenna (consecrated 547), Justinian and Theodora appear in mosaic with golden nimbi, standing near Christ, who is distinguished by a nimbus marked with a cross. Christian theology gave such imagery a precise content: the emperor’s halo indicated office and divine appointment rather than personal sanctity, while Christ’s cruciform nimbus, often inscribed with Ο ΩΝ (‘He who is’, Exodus 3:14), proclaimed his divinity.

Medieval art elaborated a code. Christ alone received the cruciform nimbus; living persons, such as Pope Paschal I in the mosaics of Santa Prassede in Rome (817–824), were given a square nimbus to distinguish them from saints in heaven; the Holy Spirit as a dove and the Lamb could also be nimbate. The Byzantine painters’ manual of Dionysius of Fourna (c. 1730) still prescribed these conventions. In the Latin West the halo shrank in the Renaissance to a thin gold ring and was sometimes abandoned for naturalistic light, a change accelerated by Protestant art, which seldom used haloes at all.

Polemical writers, from some Reformation critics of ‘popish’ images to Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853), argued that the halo exposed saint-veneration as sun worship. Modern historians of art such as Robin Jensen, André Grabar and Sabine MacCormack see a more ordinary process: Christians used the established visual vocabulary of the late Roman world to express biblical ideas of glory, and in doing so absorbed some of the imperial ideology of the age.
howItHappened: Radiate crowns and haloes were standard attributes of solar and other deities in Hellenistic and Roman art.
From the third century emperors were increasingly shown nimbate, making the nimbus a general sign of exalted status.
After Constantine, Christian artists working in the same imperial visual culture gave the nimbus first to Christ, then to angels, Mary and saints.
Biblical texts about shining faces and divine glory supplied a Christian rationale for the borrowed form.
Byzantine and medieval convention fixed distinctions: cruciform nimbus for Christ, round for saints, square for the living.
examples: Missorium of Theodosius I (388), Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid: emperors with nimbi.
Mosaics of Justinian and Theodora with nimbi, San Vitale, Ravenna (547).
Christ with cruciform nimbus in the apse of San Vitale and in Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna (sixth century).
Square nimbus of Pope Paschal I and of Theodora, mother of Paschal, in Santa Prassede, Rome (817–824).
Sixth-century Sinai icon of Christ Pantocrator, with a jewelled cruciform nimbus.

defenders.name: John of Damascus
defenders.text: Defended images of Christ and the saints as windows on divine glory (On the Divine Images, c. 730), providing the theology within which haloed icons were justified.

defenders.name: Dionysius of Fourna
defenders.text: His Painter’s Manual (Hermeneia, c. 1730) codified the Byzantine use of the cruciform nimbus inscribed Ο ΩΝ for Christ.

critics.name: Huldrych Zwingli
critics.text: Oversaw the removal of images of Christ and the saints from Zurich’s churches in 1524, rejecting the visual cult of the saints as idolatry.

critics.name: Alexander Hislop
critics.text: In The Two Babylons (1853; enlarged 1858) claimed the halo was a Babylonian sun symbol, a thesis rejected by historians but still widely repeated.

keptBy: Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox iconography, where the nimbus is obligatory for Christ, the Theotokos and the saints.
Catholic devotional and liturgical art.
Anglican and some Lutheran church art, especially in stained glass.
rejectedBy: Reformed and Puritan churches, which removed images of saints altogether.
Some modern ‘pagan origins’ polemicists, following Hislop, who regard the halo as a sun-worship symbol.

influences.name: Christ Pantocrator, imperial ceremony and Byzantine art
influences.sourceCulture: Roman imperial portraiture and court ceremonial: the enthroned ruler, purple and gold, proskynesis, the adventus procession, and the enthroned Zeus/Jupiter type
influences.christianForm: Christ enthroned as heavenly emperor and Pantocrator (‘Ruler of all’), the Maiestas Domini, and courtly elements in liturgy and icon
influences.evidenceNote: That late Roman imperial art and ceremony shaped images of Christ enthroned and some elements of liturgy is widely accepted; how far is debated. André Grabar’s classic ‘imperial’ thesis has been challenged by Thomas Mathews, who argues that images of Christ drew more on pagan gods and philosophers than on emperors. The title Pantokrator itself is biblical, not pagan.
influences.popularClaim: Once Constantine converted, the humble Jesus was turned into a Roman emperor and Christianity became an imperial religion modelled on the cult of Caesar.
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Christian art after 313 did adopt forms from the court: Christ appears enthroned in gold and purple among apostles dressed as senators (Santa Pudenziana, c. 400), Palm Sunday scenes echo the imperial adventus, and gestures such as proskynesis passed into Byzantine devotion. But Pantokrator is the Septuagint’s translation of ‘Lord of hosts’ and ‘Almighty’ and appears in Revelation 1:8, so the idea of Christ as universal ruler predates any imperial influence. The bearded, enthroned Christ also echoes Phidias’s Zeus and images of philosophers, as Mathews stresses, and Christians often used imperial forms to relativise the emperor, who in mosaics bows before Christ. Scholars therefore speak of a two-way exchange in which court culture and the church borrowed from each other.
influences.summary: From the late fourth century Christ was increasingly shown as an enthroned, majestic ruler, drawing on Roman imperial and divine imagery; the biblical title Pantocrator was given visual form in the domes and icons of Byzantium.
influences.story:
Before Constantine, images of Christ were modest: a young shepherd, a teacher, a miracle-worker with a wand. After 313, and especially from the reign of Theodosius I (379–395), a new image appeared: Christ enthroned, bearded, robed in gold, surrounded by attendants. In the apse of Santa Pudenziana in Rome (c. 390–417) he sits on a jewelled throne with the heavenly Jerusalem behind him, and the apostles, in togas, resemble a senate. André Grabar’s L’Empereur dans l’art byzantin (1936) and his later Christian Iconography (1968) argued that such images were modelled directly on imperial art: the ruler enthroned in majesty, receiving homage, handing down the law.

Court ceremonial left marks on worship too. The emperor’s formal entry into a city (adventus), with crowds carrying branches, provided a template for depictions of Christ’s entry into Jerusalem. Proskynesis, the full prostration before the emperor adopted at court in the age of Diocletian, became a normal act of reverence before icons and the altar. Lights, incense and the carrying of the Gospel book in procession resembled honours paid to the emperor’s image and to magistrates. Sabine MacCormack’s Art and Ceremony in Late Antiquity traced how these rituals and their images moved between palace and church.

The Byzantine Pantocrator was the mature fruit of this development. The sixth-century encaustic icon at St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai, shows Christ holding a jewelled Gospel book and blessing, his face subtly asymmetrical to suggest his two natures. After iconoclasm (726–843) the bust of the Pantocrator came to dominate the central domes of Byzantine churches, as at Daphni near Athens (c. 1100), and Norman Sicily imported the type into the apses of Cefalù (1148) and Monreale. In the Latin West the corresponding image was the Maiestas Domini, Christ enthroned within a mandorla among the four living creatures.

Yet the influence was not one-way, and its extent is disputed. Thomas Mathews, in The Clash of Gods (1993), argued that the ‘emperor mystique’ had been exaggerated: Christ’s long hair and beard echo Zeus and Asclepius, his miracles resemble the magician’s, and his teaching pose is that of the philosopher; early artists were competing with the pagan gods more than flattering the emperor. The word Pantokrator itself comes from the Greek Bible, where it renders ‘Lord of hosts’ (Sabaoth) and ‘Almighty’, and from Revelation 1:8. Imperial imagery could also be used to subordinate the emperor: in Hagia Sophia an emperor, probably Leo VI, prostrates himself before the enthroned Christ (late ninth or early tenth century).

The theological interpretation of this marriage has always divided Christians. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his oration for Constantine’s thirty years (336), saw the Christian empire as an image of the heavenly monarchy of the Logos, an outlook that shaped Byzantine political theology. Critics of the ‘Constantinian’ church, from medieval dissenters and Anabaptists to modern theologians, have argued that the imperial Christ obscured the crucified one. Historians generally conclude that the church took over the visual and ceremonial language of power available to it, while biblical and doctrinal content, especially the confession of Christ as fully divine at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451), determined what that language was made to say.
howItHappened: After 313 Christian patrons, including emperors and aristocrats, commissioned church decoration from artists trained in imperial and civic art.
The Nicene confession of Christ as fully divine encouraged images that showed him as cosmic ruler rather than only as teacher or shepherd.
Court rituals of adventus, proskynesis and honour to the imperial image provided models for liturgical processions and veneration of icons.
Byzantine theology of the Christian empire, from Eusebius onwards, presented the emperor as earthly image of Christ’s heavenly rule.
After iconoclasm, the Pantocrator bust became the standard dome image of the Byzantine church interior.
examples: Apse mosaic of Santa Pudenziana, Rome (c. 390–417): Christ enthroned among apostles in senatorial dress.
Encaustic icon of Christ Pantocrator, St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai (sixth century).
Apse of San Vitale, Ravenna (547): a youthful Christ seated on the globe, offering a crown to St Vitalis.
Narthex mosaic of an emperor (probably Leo VI) prostrate before Christ, Hagia Sophia, Constantinople (c. 886–912).
Dome Pantocrator at Daphni monastery, near Athens (c. 1100), and apse Pantocrator at Cefalù cathedral, Sicily (1148).

defenders.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
defenders.text: In his Tricennial Oration (336) and Life of Constantine presented the Christian emperor as image of the Logos’s heavenly monarchy, the foundation of Byzantine political theology.

defenders.name: John of Damascus
defenders.text: Used the analogy of honour paid to the emperor’s image to explain why veneration of an icon passes to Christ himself (On the Divine Images).

critics.name: Constantine V
critics.text: The iconoclast emperor argued in his Peuseis (c. 750s) that Christ, being divine, could not be truly portrayed, and attacked the cult of images.

critics.name: Thomas F. Mathews
critics.text: Art historian whose The Clash of Gods (1993) argued against the ‘imperial’ interpretation, tracing images of Christ to pagan gods, magicians and philosophers instead.

keptBy: Eastern Orthodox churches, where the Pantocrator in the dome and on the iconostasis is central to the church’s visual theology.
Eastern Catholic churches of the Byzantine rite.
Catholic and Anglican art in the form of Christ in Majesty, Christ the King (feast instituted 1925).
rejectedBy: Byzantine iconoclasts (726–787, 815–843), who rejected images of Christ.
Reformed and other Protestant traditions that exclude images of Christ from worship.
Anabaptist and other critics of ‘Constantinian’ Christianity, who reject the imperial model of Christ and church.

influences.name: Mary, Isis and the mother-goddess debate
influences.sourceCulture: Isis nursing the infant Horus (Isis lactans) and the titles and devotions of Isis and other mother goddesses
influences.christianForm: Images of the Virgin and Child, especially the nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa), and Marian titles and devotion
influences.evidenceNote: Some iconographic influence of Isis-and-Horus images on Egyptian and Byzantine images of the nursing Virgin is plausible and argued by respected art historians. That Marian doctrine or devotion originated in the Isis cult is not supported: it grew from the Gospels, the second-century Protevangelium of James and the fifth-century debates about Christ. Claims that Mary is simply Isis, Ishtar or Semiramis renamed belong to polemic, not historical evidence.
influences.popularClaim: The Virgin Mary is the Egyptian goddess Isis (or the Babylonian ‘Queen of Heaven’) in Christian dress: the Madonna and Child were copied from Isis and Horus, and the church adopted a mother goddess to win pagans.
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Historians distinguish image from belief. Visually, the seated mother suckling a divine child was an established Egyptian type, and Thomas Mathews and Norman Muller have argued that painted Isis panels were among the models for early Marian icons; Coptic Galaktotrophousa images strengthen the case. But the mother-and-child pose is near-universal, and the earliest Christian example (Catacomb of Priscilla, third century) is not Egyptian. Marian devotion has clear Christian roots: the infancy narratives, the Protevangelium of James (c. 150), the Eve–Mary typology of Justin and Irenaeus, and the title Theotokos, defended by Cyril of Alexandria and proclaimed at Ephesus in 431 to safeguard the unity of Christ. Church leaders also explicitly opposed goddess-like worship of Mary, as Epiphanius did with the Collyridians. Scholars such as R. E. Witt argued for strong Isiac influence on popular piety, while Stephen Shoemaker, Hilda Graef and Jaroslav Pelikan locate the origins of Marian devotion within Christian tradition; the debate is real but concerns influence on forms of piety and art, not the source of the doctrine.
influences.summary: Images of the Virgin nursing the Christ child resemble Egyptian images of Isis nursing Horus, and scholars debate the extent of artistic and devotional influence; the popular claim that Mary is a renamed Isis is not supported by evidence.
influences.story:
Isis was one of the most popular deities of the Roman Empire. Her cult spread from Egypt across the Mediterranean, with temples in Rome, Pompeii and London; Apuleius’s Golden Ass (book 11, second century) gives a famous hymn to her as queen of heaven and mother of all. Egyptian art had for many centuries shown her seated, suckling the infant Horus, and her worshippers celebrated her as protector of seafarers (Isis Pelagia), healer and saviour. At Philae in Upper Egypt her temple remained active until c. 535–537, when Justinian’s general Narses closed it; part of it was later converted into a church of St Stephen.

The resemblance between Isis lactans and images of the Virgin nursing Christ has been noticed since the Enlightenment. The earliest Christian image of Mary and the child, in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome (early to mid-third century), shows a seated woman holding an infant beside a prophet pointing to a star. In Egypt the nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa or Maria lactans) appears in Coptic wall paintings at the monasteries of Apa Jeremias at Saqqara and Apa Apollo at Bawit (sixth to seventh centuries). Thomas Mathews and Norman Muller argued in 2005 that late-antique painted panels of Isis were a direct model for early Marian icons, a view many art historians find plausible for Egypt while noting that the mother-and-child pose is common to many cultures.

Marian belief, however, had its own Christian sources. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell of the virginal conception; Justin Martyr (c. 155) and Irenaeus (c. 180) developed Mary as the new Eve; the Protevangelium of James (c. 150) narrated her birth and perpetual virginity. The title Theotokos (‘God-bearer’) was used in Alexandria by the early fourth century, and the prayer Sub tuum praesidium, addressed to the Theotokos, survives on a papyrus variously dated between the third and seventh centuries. When Nestorius of Constantinople objected to the title in 428, warning against making the Virgin a goddess, Cyril of Alexandria defended it as a statement about Christ: the child Mary bore was God the Word incarnate. The Council of Ephesus (431) agreed with Cyril, and Marian devotion grew rapidly afterwards.

That the council met in Ephesus, the city of Artemis (Acts 19), has encouraged claims that the Theotokos replaced the Ephesian goddess, but the choice of venue and the outcome were driven by ecclesiastical politics and Christology. The church explicitly rejected goddess-like cult: Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 79, c. 377) condemned the Collyridians, women in Arabia who offered bread-cakes to Mary as a priestess would to a goddess, insisting that ‘Mary is to be honoured, but the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are to be worshipped’. Later titles once linked to Isis have other derivations: ‘Star of the Sea’ (Stella maris) arose from Jerome’s etymology of Miriam as ‘drop of the sea’ (stilla maris), and ‘Queen of Heaven’ (Regina caeli) developed from biblical imagery of the woman in Revelation 12 and Mary’s place in Christ’s kingdom; the ‘queen of heaven’ condemned in Jeremiah 7 and 44 was a Near Eastern goddess and was never identified with Mary by the church.

The modern debate has been sharpened by Protestant polemic. Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853) identified Mary with Semiramis and Isis as part of an attack on Roman Catholicism, and his claims still circulate though historians have long rejected his method. Scholars such as R. E. Witt (Isis in the Graeco-Roman World, 1971) argued for real Isiac influence on popular piety; others, including Stephen Shoemaker, Hilda Graef and Jaroslav Pelikan, emphasise the internal Christian development of Marian devotion. A fair summary is that late-antique Christians lived among images and devotions to divine mothers and may have borrowed artistic forms, while the content of Marian doctrine was shaped by debates about who Christ is.
howItHappened: Christian artists in Egypt and elsewhere drew on familiar images of seated mothers and divine infants, including Isis and Horus.
The Christological controversies of the fifth century made the title Theotokos a test of orthodoxy and stimulated Marian feasts, churches and images.
As pagan temples closed, some former devotees of Isis and other goddesses became Christians and may have carried habits of piety with them.
Bishops drew boundaries, distinguishing honour paid to Mary from worship due to God alone (later formalised as hyperdulia versus latria).
Protestant and Enlightenment polemicists from the seventeenth century onwards highlighted the parallels to attack Catholic devotion.
examples: Virgin and Child with a prophet, Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome (third century).
Nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa) at the Monastery of Apa Jeremias, Saqqara (sixth–seventh century), now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo.
Egyptian terracotta and bronze figurines of Isis lactans nursing Horus (Roman period).
The Temple of Isis at Philae, closed c. 535–537 and partly converted to a church.
Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome, rebuilt by Sixtus III (432–440) after the Council of Ephesus, with mosaics of Christ’s infancy.

defenders.name: Cyril of Alexandria
defenders.text: Defended the title Theotokos against Nestorius as a confession that Mary’s son is God incarnate, making Marian honour an expression of Christology.

defenders.name: John of Damascus
defenders.text: Wrote homilies on the Dormition and distinguished the honour given to the Theotokos and saints from the worship due to God alone.

critics.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
critics.text: Condemned the Collyridians for offering cakes to Mary as a goddess: ‘Let Mary be honoured, but let the Lord be worshipped’ (Panarion 79).

critics.name: Nestorius
critics.text: Objected to the title Theotokos in 428, warning that it risked making the Virgin a goddess; condemned at Ephesus in 431.

critics.name: Alexander Hislop
critics.text: His anti-Catholic The Two Babylons (1853) identified Mary with Isis and Semiramis; the book remains influential in some circles despite its discredited method.

keptBy: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, which honour Mary as Theotokos and reject the claim of pagan origin.
Anglican and Lutheran traditions, which keep some Marian feasts and the title Theotokos as defined at Ephesus.
rejectedBy: Reformed and many evangelical Protestants, who reject Marian invocation and often see parallels with goddess cults as a warning.
Jehovah’s Witnesses and some fundamentalist writers, whose literature has drawn on Hislop’s identification of Mary with pagan goddesses.

influences.name: Early symbols: fish, anchor, Chi-Rho and the cross
influences.sourceCulture: Common Graeco-Roman motifs (fish, anchor, dove, ship), the Greek chi-rho ligature used as an abbreviation, and the Roman cross as an instrument of execution
influences.christianForm: The ichthys acrostic, the anchor of hope, the Chi-Rho monogram, the staurogram and the cross as Christian emblems
influences.evidenceNote: The popular claims that the fish is a pagan fertility symbol, that the cross is the Tammuz ‘tau’ and that the Chi-Rho was a solar emblem lack evidence. What is true is that Christians used ordinary graphic forms: anchors, fish and doves were everyday motifs, and the chi-rho ligature existed as an abbreviation before Christ. Christian meanings for these symbols are explicitly documented in second- and third-century texts.
influences.popularClaim: Christian symbols are pagan in origin: the fish (ichthys) comes from the fertility cults of Atargatis or Dagon, the cross from the ‘T’ of Tammuz, and Constantine’s Chi-Rho was really a sun symbol.
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Christian authors of c. 180–230 explain the meaning of their symbols in their own words. Tertullian (De baptismo 1) and the Abercius inscription use the fish for Christ; the acrostic ΙΧΘΥΣ (‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’) appears in the Sibylline Oracles (8.217–250) quoted by Augustine; Clement of Alexandria lists the dove, fish, ship and anchor as suitable seal-ring images (Paedagogus 3.11). The anchor draws on Hebrews 6:19. The cross was the instrument of Jesus’s execution, as the Gospels and the anti-Christian Alexamenos graffito (c. 200) show, and the ‘staurogram’ appears in Gospel papyri (P66, P75) before Constantine. The chi-rho ligature had been used on Ptolemaic coins and as a scribal mark, and Constantine adopted it as Christ’s monogram in 312 according to Lactantius. Historians see the reuse of everyday graphic forms, not the adoption of pagan religious symbols.
influences.summary: The first Christian symbols, the fish, anchor, dove, Chi-Rho and cross, used ordinary forms of the Roman world but had explicitly Christian meanings attested in early texts; claims of pagan religious origin do not stand up to the evidence.
influences.story:
Before Christians made pictures of Christ they used signs. Clement of Alexandria, writing c. 200, told believers that their seal rings should not bear idols, swords or wine-cups but a dove, a fish, a ship running before the wind, a lyre or an anchor, and that a fisherman would remind them of the apostles and the children drawn from the water (Paedagogus 3.11). The list shows both continuity and choice: these were stock motifs of Roman gem-cutters, selected because they could carry Christian meaning.

The fish is the best documented. The Greek word ΙΧΘΥΣ forms an acrostic of Iēsous Christos Theou Huios Sōtēr, ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’, worked into an acrostic poem in the Sibylline Oracles (8.217–250) which Augustine later quoted (City of God 18.23). Tertullian wrote c. 200 that ‘we little fishes, after the example of our Ichthys Jesus Christ, are born in water’ (De baptismo 1). The epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis in Phrygia (before 216) speaks of eating ‘the fish from the spring, very great and pure’, and the Pectorius inscription at Autun uses the same imagery. Gospel stories of fishermen, the feeding of the multitudes and the risen Christ’s meal of fish reinforced the symbol. The Syrian goddess Atargatis did have sacred fish, as Lucian notes, but there is no evidence that Christians drew on her cult.

The anchor, common on pagan tombstones as a sailor’s emblem, became for Christians the ‘anchor of the soul’ (Hebrews 6:19), often shaped so that its stock suggested a cross; it is frequent in the Catacomb of Priscilla and on early epitaphs. The dove carried the olive branch of Noah and the Spirit of Jesus’s baptism. The cross itself was rarely depicted before the fourth century: Roman crucifixion was a shameful death, and a graffito on the Palatine (c. 200) mocks a Christian named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head. Yet Christians traced the sign of the cross on their foreheads (Tertullian, De corona 3); Justin Martyr saw the cross shape everywhere in nature, in masts, ploughs and the human form (1 Apology 55); and Minucius Felix insisted that Christians did not worship crosses (Octavius 29). Larry Hurtado and Bruce Longenecker have shown that the staurogram, a tau-rho ligature depicting the crucified Jesus, was used in Christian manuscripts c. 200 and that cross imagery existed before Constantine.

The Chi-Rho monogram, formed from the first two Greek letters of Christos, came to prominence with Constantine. Lactantius, a contemporary, reports that before the battle of the Milvian Bridge (312) Constantine was told in a dream to mark ‘the heavenly sign of God’ on his soldiers’ shields, a letter X with its top bent round, i.e. the Chi-Rho (De mortibus persecutorum 44). Eusebius’s later account describes a vision of a cross of light with the words ‘By this conquer’ and the jewelled standard, the labarum (Life of Constantine 1.28–31). The ligature itself was not new: it appears on coins of Ptolemy III and as a scribe’s abbreviation for chrēston (‘useful’). Constantine’s silver medallion from Ticinum (c. 315) shows the Chi-Rho on his helmet, and the monogram was soon ubiquitous on sarcophagi, lamps and church furnishings.

In the modern era some groups have rejected the cross as pagan. Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853) traced it to the Tammuz ‘tau’, and from the 1930s Jehovah’s Witnesses abandoned the cross, teaching that Jesus died on an upright stake (‘torture stake’ in the New World Translation). Historians note that Greek stauros and Latin crux were used of crosses of several shapes, that Roman sources describe crucifixion with a crossbeam (patibulum), and that early Christian writers already took the cross shape for granted. The borrowing in this story is of forms: an alphabet, a vocabulary of motifs and a Roman instrument of death, given new meaning by a community that proclaimed a crucified Messiah.
howItHappened: Christians chose from the existing repertoire of Roman gem, lamp and tomb motifs those that could bear Christian meaning.
Wordplay and acrostics, such as ΙΧΘΥΣ, gave ordinary images a confessional content intelligible to insiders.
Biblical texts (Hebrews 6:19, Genesis 8, the Gospel fish stories) supplied the meanings of the anchor, dove and fish.
Scribes developed the nomina sacra and the staurogram, turning letter combinations into visual references to Christ and his cross.
Constantine’s adoption of the Chi-Rho in 312 made Christian symbols public, imperial and military.
examples: Fish and bread-basket paintings in the Crypts of Lucina, Catacomb of Callixtus, Rome (early third century).
Epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis (late second century), fragments in the Vatican Museums.
Anchors and fish on third-century epitaphs in the Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome.
Staurogram in the Bodmer papyri P66 and P75 (c. 175–225).
Alexamenos graffito, Palatine Hill, Rome (c. 200).
Chi-Rho on Constantine’s helmet on the Ticinum silver medallion (c. 315), and on fourth-century ‘passion’ sarcophagi.

defenders.name: Clement of Alexandria
defenders.text: Recommended the dove, fish, ship, lyre and anchor as seal-ring images, reinterpreting common motifs for Christian use (Paedagogus 3.11).

defenders.name: Tertullian
defenders.text: Explained the fish as a baptismal symbol (De baptismo 1) and described Christians signing their foreheads with the cross (De corona 3).

defenders.name: Justin Martyr
defenders.text: Argued that the shape of the cross was imprinted throughout nature and human culture, from ships’ masts to military standards (1 Apology 55).

defenders.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
defenders.text: Recorded Constantine’s vision and described the labarum with its Chi-Rho (Life of Constantine 1.28–31).

critics.name: Alexander Hislop
critics.text: Claimed in The Two Babylons (1853) that the cross derived from the mystic ‘tau’ of Tammuz, an assertion without ancient evidence.

critics.name: Jehovah’s Witnesses
critics.text: Since the 1930s have rejected the cross as a pagan symbol, teaching that Jesus died on a single upright stake.

keptBy: Virtually all Christian traditions use the cross; Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental and Anglican churches also use the crucifix.
Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches use the Chi-Rho on vestments, altars and Easter candles.
Many modern Protestants use the ichthys as a badge of faith.
rejectedBy: Jehovah’s Witnesses, who reject the cross.
Some Reformed and Puritan Christians, who removed crucifixes and cross ornaments from churches as idolatrous, while keeping the doctrine of the cross.

influences.name: The basilica: Roman civic halls become churches
influences.sourceCulture: The Roman basilica: a large rectangular hall with aisles and an apse, used for law courts, commerce and imperial audiences
influences.christianForm: The aisled basilica church with nave, apse, altar and bishop’s throne (cathedra), the standard form of Western church building
influences.evidenceNote: The derivation of the Christian basilica from Roman secular halls is one of the best-documented borrowings in the history of Christianity. The very name was taken over, Constantine’s first great churches are basilicas, and their plans are closely comparable to forensic and palatine halls. Scholars debate only which secular hall type was the main model, not the borrowing itself.
influences.popularClaim: Church buildings are a pagan invention: the first Christians met only in homes, and when Constantine built basilicas he turned the church into a copy of pagan temples (as argued, for example, in Viola and Barna’s Pagan Christianity?, 2008).
influences.whatHistoriansSay: Historians agree that the early church met in houses and then in adapted house churches (domus ecclesiae), such as at Dura-Europos (c. 232–256), and that monumental church architecture began with Constantine after 312. But the model was the civic basilica, not the temple. Roman temples housed a cult statue and sacrifices took place outside at an altar; Christian worship needed a large interior space for an assembly hearing Scripture and sharing the Eucharist, which the basilica provided. Richard Krautheimer emphasised the imperial audience hall as a model, while L. Michael White traced a gradual development from house to hall. The basilica is therefore a borrowing of architectural form for Christian purposes, and Christians deliberately avoided the temple type.
influences.summary: From 312 Constantine and his successors housed Christian worship in basilicas, the multi-purpose public halls of Roman cities, giving Western Christianity its characteristic long, aisled church with an apse.
influences.story:
The Greek word basilikē (‘royal’ hall) had by the second century BC become the name of a type of Roman public building: a large roofed hall, often divided by colonnades into a central nave and side aisles, lit by clerestory windows, with a raised tribunal, frequently in an apse, from which magistrates presided. The Basilica Ulpia in Trajan’s Forum (dedicated 112) and the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine (completed c. 313) in Rome were among the grandest. Vitruvius described the type and his own basilica at Fanum (De architectura 5.1), and in the early fourth century Constantine built a vast brick audience hall at Trier, the Aula Palatina.

Before 312 Christians had no such buildings. They met in private houses and, from the third century, in houses remodelled for worship, of which the best preserved is at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, with an assembly room and a painted baptistery. Some congregations had larger halls by the late third century, since the Great Persecution of 303 began with the destruction of a church at Nicomedia, but there was no monumental Christian architecture. Early apologists such as Minucius Felix even boasted that Christians had ‘no temples and no altars’ (Octavius 32).

Constantine’s patronage changed this. Soon after his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) he gave the Lateran palace to the bishop of Rome and built beside it the Basilica Constantiniana, now St John Lateran, a five-aisled hall with an apse. Old St Peter’s on the Vatican (begun c. 319–322), the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem (dedicated 335) and the Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem followed. Eusebius’s panegyric on the new cathedral at Tyre (c. 315–317, Ecclesiastical History 10.4) describes its atrium, nave and aisles, raised thrones for the clergy and altar. The bishop’s chair (cathedra) stood where the magistrate had sat in the apse, giving the word ‘cathedral’, and the altar stood before it.

The choice of the basilica was deliberate. Temples were the houses of gods and their images, small interior spaces with public sacrifice outside; Christian worship gathered the whole community inside for readings, preaching and the Eucharist. The basilica was a neutral, prestigious, flexible public building, already associated with imperial authority and justice, and suited to large congregations and processions. Richard Krautheimer stressed the influence of imperial audience halls in which the emperor received homage; others emphasise forensic and commercial basilicas or, like L. Michael White, a gradual evolution from house church to hall. At Aquileia the twin halls built by Bishop Theodore (c. 313–319) show an intermediate stage.

The basilica remained the norm in the Latin West through the Romanesque and Gothic eras, while the Byzantine East developed the domed centralised church and the cross-in-square. Its civic origin has been read in different ways: as a fitting expression of the church’s public role, or as the beginning of a ‘Constantinian’ church of wealth and power. Jerome already complained that churches glittered with marble and gold while Christ starved at the door in the person of the poor (Letter 52.10). Puritans and Quakers later built plain meeting houses, and modern house-church advocates have revived the argument that church buildings are a departure from the New Testament. Historically, the basilica is a clear case of borrowing an architectural form rather than a religious practice.
howItHappened: Christians had worshipped in houses and adapted house churches, so there was no existing Christian monumental type.
After 312 Constantine funded large churches in Rome, the Holy Land and Constantinople and his architects used the familiar public hall.
The basilica’s nave, aisles and apse suited a large assembly, processions and a presiding bishop.
Christians deliberately avoided the temple form, which was associated with cult statues and sacrifice.
Imperial and civic features, such as the apse tribunal and throne, were adapted for the bishop’s cathedra and the altar.
examples: Basilica Ulpia, Forum of Trajan, Rome (112): the classic civic basilica.
Aula Palatina, Trier (c. 310): an imperial audience hall, later used as a Protestant church (from 1856).
Dura-Europos house church (c. 232–256): worship before monumental churches.
Basilica Constantiniana (St John Lateran), Rome (begun c. 312).
Old St Peter’s, Rome (begun c. 319–322); Santa Sabina, Rome (c. 422–432), the best-preserved early basilica.
Twin halls of Bishop Theodore at Aquileia (c. 313–319), with their floor mosaics.

defenders.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
defenders.text: Praised the new basilica at Tyre as a fitting temple of God and an image of the church (Ecclesiastical History 10.4).

defenders.name: Constantine I
defenders.text: Commissioned the Lateran, St Peter’s, the Holy Sepulchre and other basilicas, instructing bishops to build churches worthy of the empire (Life of Constantine 2.46, 3.31).

critics.name: Jerome
critics.text: Complained that churches gleamed with marble and gold while Christ starved at the door in the poor (Letter 52.10).

critics.name: Frank Viola and George Barna
critics.text: In Pagan Christianity? (2008) argued that church buildings derive from pagan and Constantinian practice and urged a return to house churches.

keptBy: Catholic churches, where ‘basilica’ is also an honorific title granted by the pope.
Anglican, Lutheran and many other Western churches, whose parish churches descend from the basilican plan.
Eastern Orthodox churches, which used basilicas before developing the domed cross-in-square type.
rejectedBy: Puritans and Congregationalists, who built plain meeting houses rather than ‘churches’ in the medieval form.
Quakers, who reject consecrated buildings in favour of meeting houses.
Modern house-church movements, which regard dedicated church buildings as unnecessary or unbiblical.

influences.name: Temples turned into churches (Pantheon, Parthenon) and Gregory’s letter to Mellitus
influences.sourceCulture: Pagan temples, shrines and festival customs of Rome, Greece, Egypt and Anglo-Saxon England
influences.christianForm: Former temples consecrated as churches, and Gregory the Great’s policy of reusing shrines and festivals for Christian worship
influences.evidenceNote: The conversion of particular temples into churches is securely documented (the Pantheon in 609, the Parthenon probably in the late sixth century), and Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus of 601, preserved by Bede, explicitly advises adapting pagan shrines and festivals. What is overstated is the scale: temple conversions were relatively few and mostly late, often after buildings had stood empty for generations.
influences.popularClaim: Christians systematically built their churches on top of pagan temples, so that Christian worship is pagan worship continued under new names (or, conversely, that Christians simply destroyed every temple).
influences.whatHistoriansSay: R. P. C. Hanson’s survey (1978) and later archaeology (Lavan and Mulryan, 2011) show that direct conversion of temples into churches was less common and later than often assumed: imperial laws closed temples from 391–392 and ordered their destruction or cleansing in 435 (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.25), but many buildings decayed or were quarried, some were violently destroyed (the Serapeum of Alexandria, 391/392), and only a minority became churches, mostly in the sixth and seventh centuries. The most famous cases are real and well documented. Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus is genuine evidence for a deliberate missionary strategy of adapting buildings and customs, though Gregory had written a month earlier urging King Æthelberht to destroy shrines, and archaeological evidence for reused shrines in England is thin. Reuse of sites and buildings expressed the victory of Christ over the gods; it did not mean the continuity of pagan worship.
influences.summary: Some famous pagan temples, including the Pantheon in Rome and the Parthenon in Athens, became churches, and in 601 Gregory the Great advised missionaries in England to purify and reuse pagan shrines and turn festivals into Christian feasts; such reuse was real but less widespread and later than popularly supposed.
influences.story:
In the fourth century Christian emperors moved gradually from tolerating to suppressing public pagan cult. Constantine stripped some temples of treasures; Theodosius I’s laws of 391–392 banned sacrifice and closed temples; and a law of 435 ordered surviving shrines to be destroyed and purified by the sign of the cross (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.25). Practice varied. In some cities bishops and monks destroyed temples: Marcellus of Apamea pulled down the temple of Zeus c. 386, Theophilus of Alexandria oversaw the destruction of the Serapeum in 391 or 392, and Martin of Tours demolished shrines in Gaul. The pagan orator Libanius protested to Theodosius (Oration 30, Pro templis) against monks who wrecked rural temples.

Conversion into churches was a different process, and generally later. R. P. C. Hanson’s survey found relatively few clear examples before the sixth century: Christians were often reluctant to worship in buildings they regarded as haunted by demons, and temple interiors were ill-suited to congregational worship. Notable conversions include the Temple of Isis at Philae (after c. 535–537), the Hephaisteion in Athens (as a church of St George) and the Temple of Athena at Syracuse, which became the cathedral, its columns still visible in the walls. The Parthenon was converted into a church of the Theotokos, probably in the late sixth century, and was the cathedral of Athens for centuries, a major pilgrimage site in Byzantine times according to Anthony Kaldellis.

The Pantheon in Rome is the classic case. According to the Liber Pontificalis, Pope Boniface IV obtained the disused temple from the emperor Phocas and dedicated it on 13 May 609 (or 610) as Santa Maria ad Martyres, translating martyrs’ relics into it. It is the main reason the building survives intact. In Rome, too, the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina became San Lorenzo in Miranda, and the Curia, the Senate house, became the church of Sant’Adriano in the seventh century.

The theory behind such reuse was articulated by Gregory the Great. Writing to Abbot Mellitus on 18 July 601, as he set out to join Augustine’s mission in Kent, Gregory revised his earlier advice to King Æthelberht to destroy shrines. The temples of the English, he wrote, should not be destroyed but cleansed of their idols, sprinkled with holy water and furnished with altars and relics, so that the people would come more readily to familiar places; and because they had been used to sacrificing oxen to demons, they should instead hold feasts in booths of branches on the days of dedication or of the martyrs, killing animals for food in praise of God. ‘It is impossible to cut off everything at once from hard hearts’, he explained, ‘for whoever wishes to climb to the highest place rises by steps, not by leaps’ (Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30). Augustine of Hippo had earlier allowed temples to be converted ‘to the worship of the true God’ (Letter 47.3), and his principle of ‘spoiling the Egyptians’ (On Christian Teaching 2.40.60) offered a wider rationale for taking over what was good in pagan culture.

How far Gregory’s policy was carried out is uncertain. Bede also records the high priest Coifi profaning and burning the temple at Goodmanham (2.13) and King Rædwald keeping a Christian altar and a pagan one in the same shrine (2.15), and archaeologists have found few clear Anglo-Saxon churches on pagan cult buildings. The letter has nonetheless become the classic text for both admirers of missionary adaptation and critics of Christian ‘paganisation’, from Conyers Middleton’s Letter from Rome (1729) onwards. Historians now treat it as evidence of a pragmatic, gradualist strategy in which reuse of place and custom signalled Christ’s victory over the old gods, rather than a wholesale continuation of pagan religion.
howItHappened: Imperial laws of 391–392 and 435 closed temples and ordered their destruction or purification, leaving many buildings empty.
Some temples were destroyed by bishops, monks and crowds; others decayed or were quarried for materials.
From the sixth century prominent temples, often long disused, were consecrated as churches, usually with relics of martyrs.
Popes and emperors granted temple buildings to the church, as Phocas gave the Pantheon to Boniface IV.
Gregory the Great formulated a missionary policy of cleansing and reusing shrines and replacing sacrificial feasts with Christian festivals (601).
examples: The Pantheon, Rome, dedicated as Santa Maria ad Martyres by Boniface IV (609/610).
The Parthenon, Athens, converted to a church of the Theotokos (probably late sixth century), later a Latin cathedral (1204) and a mosque (after 1460).
The Temple of Athena, Syracuse, incorporated into the cathedral (seventh century).
The Temple of Isis at Philae, Egypt, partly converted into a church after its closure c. 535–537.
The Serapeum of Alexandria, destroyed in 391/392: the alternative fate.
Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus (601), preserved in Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30.

defenders.name: Gregory the Great
defenders.text: Advised that English temples be cleansed and reused as churches and that sacrificial feasts become Christian festivals, rising ‘by steps, not by leaps’ (Letter to Mellitus, 601).

defenders.name: Augustine of Hippo
defenders.text: Allowed temples to be turned to the worship of the true God (Letter 47.3) and taught that Christians should take over pagan learning as Israel ‘spoiled the Egyptians’ (On Christian Teaching 2.40.60).

defenders.name: Bede
defenders.text: Preserved Gregory’s letters and presented the gradual Christianisation of English sacred places as a model of missionary wisdom (Ecclesiastical History, 731).

critics.name: Libanius
critics.text: Pagan orator who protested to Theodosius I against monks destroying rural temples (Oration 30, c. 386).

critics.name: Conyers Middleton
critics.text: Anglican clergyman whose A Letter from Rome (1729) argued that Roman Catholic worship was continuous with paganism, citing temples turned into churches.

keptBy: Catholic Church, which still uses the Pantheon and other converted temples as churches.
Eastern Orthodox churches, which used converted temples in Greece and the Near East.
Catholic and Anglican missiology, which cites Gregory’s letter as a precedent for inculturation.
rejectedBy: Many Protestant polemicists since the Reformation, who saw such adaptation as the paganisation of the church.
Some early Christian zealots, who preferred to destroy temples rather than reuse them.
